## Data Wrangling

```{r}
#This chunk is intended to combine the no3 and climind df
# 1. Read the CSV files into R
kelp_data <- read.csv("kelp_no3_waves_quarterly_long.csv")
clim_data <- read.csv("climind_quarterly.csv")

# 2. Combine the data frames
combined_sitespecific_climind <- left_join(kelp_data, clim_data, by = c("year", "quarter"))

# View the new dataframe
head(combined_sitespecific_climind)
```

```{r}
# Save the combined data frame as a new CSV file
write.csv(combined_sitespecific_climind, file = "newdf/combined_kelp_climind_data.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#this chunk is to create a new df with temp included
# 1. Read the temperature data
temp_data <- read.csv("SBH_temperature_20241231.csv")

# 2. Convert daily data to quarterly averages
temp_quarterly <- temp_data %>%
  # Create a "quarter" column based on the MONTH (e.g., Jan-Mar = 1, Apr-Jun = 2, etc.)
  mutate(quarter = ceiling(MONTH / 3)) %>%
  # Rename YEAR to lowercase "year" so it matches your other datasets
  rename(year = YEAR) %>%
  # Group by the year and our newly created quarter
  group_by(year, quarter) %>%
  # Calculate the average surface temperature for that quarter (ignoring missing data)
  summarize(mean_surf_temp = mean(SURF_TEMP_C, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# 3. Join the new quarterly temperature data to your combined dataframe
combined_sitespecific_climind_temp <- left_join(combined_sitespecific_climind, temp_quarterly, by = c("year", "quarter"))

# View the results to make sure 'mean_surf_temp' was added
head(combined_sitespecific_climind_temp)

#save df as file
write.csv(combined_sitespecific_climind_temp, file = "newdf/combined_sitespecific_climind_temp.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```



```{r}

p.basic.annual.nitrate
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-hexbin-annual
#| fig-cap: "Hexagonal binning showing the density of observations for kelp abundance and nitrate."

ggplot(data = kelp_no3_annual, aes(x = no3, y = kelp)) +
  geom_hex(bins = 30) + # Adjust 'bins' to make hexes larger or smaller
  scale_fill_viridis_c() + # A visually appealing, colorblind-friendly scale
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Density of Kelp Abundance vs. Nitrate",
    x = "Nitrate Concentration (NO3)",
    y = "Kelp Abundance",
    fill = "Count"
  )
```

### Finding what model fits best using PSIS and WAIC

##### Linear

###### Linear Model NO3 Vs. Kelp Biomass

```{r}
m.biomass.nitrate <- 
  brm(data = kelp_no3_quarterly, # Give the model the Kelp/nitrate data
      # Choose a gaussian (normal) distribution
      family = gaussian,
      # Specify the model here. 
      kelp ~ no3,
      # Here's where you specify parameters for executing the Markov chains
      # We're using similar to the defaults, except we set cores to 4 so the analysis runs faster than the default of 1
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
      # Setting the "seed" determines which random numbers will get sampled.
      # In this case, it makes the randomness of the Markov chain runs reproducible 
      # (so that both of us get the exact same results when running the model)
      seed = 4,
      # Save the fitted model object as output - helpful for reloading in the output later
      file = "outputs/m.biomass.nitrate")
```

```{r}
summary(m.biomass.nitrate)
plot(m.biomass.nitrate)
```


##### Multiple Regression

##### Finding what variables impact Nitrate Levels (Adjustment direct effect)

```{r}
#THIS IS FOR THE DAG WITHOUT MEI PDO AND NPGO CONNECTED TO WAVE HEIGHT
#estimating the direct effect of NPGO, PDO, Temperature, and MEI on Nitrate:
m.nitrate.MEI.NPGO.PDO.Temp <- 
  brm(data = combined_sitespecific_climind_temp, # Give the model the combined data
      # Choose a gaussian (normal) distribution
      family = gaussian,
      # Specify the model here. 
      no3 ~ NPGO + MEI + mean_surf_temp,
      # Here's where you specify parameters for executing the Markov chains
      # We're using similar to the defaults, except we set cores to 4 so the analysis runs faster than the default of 1
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
      # Setting the "seed" determines which random numbers will get sampled.
      # In this case, it makes the randomness of the Markov chain runs reproducible 
      # (so that both of us get the exact same results when running the model)
      seed = 4,
      # Save the fitted model object as output - helpful for reloading in the output later
      file = "outputs/m.nitrate.MEI.NPGO.PDO.Temp")

summary(m.nitrate.NPGO.PDO.Temp)
plot(m.nitrate.NPGO.PDO.Temp)
```
